clinicalPearls: A rare subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease defined by autoantibodies against a 200 kDa protein in the lower lamina lucida, identified in many cases as laminin gamma-1.
Clinically it often resembles bullous pemphigoid with tense blisters on an urticarial or erythematous base, but lesions may favour the palms, soles and acral sites.
A subset of patients show features overlapping with dermatitis herpetiformis, and mucosal involvement can occur, broadening the clinical differential.
An association with psoriasis is reported in a notable proportion of patients, which may precede or accompany the blistering eruption.
Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement-membrane zone, indistinguishable from other pemphigoid variants on routine testing.

On salt-split skin indirect immunofluorescence, autoantibodies bind the dermal (floor) side of the split, as in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, so serological confirmation by immunoblot is needed to distinguish them.
Diagnosis is confirmed by immunoblotting serum against dermal extract, revealing reactivity with a 200 kDa band (and often laminin gamma-1).
The disease generally responds well to topical or systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents, and tends to be less refractory than epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
reference.pathophysiology: Anti-p200 pemphigoid is caused by circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against a 200 kDa acidic glycoprotein located in the lower portion of the lamina lucida at the dermo-epidermal junction; in a large proportion of patients this antigen has been characterised as laminin gamma-1, a constituent of several laminin isoforms. Antibody binding, with subsequent complement activation and neutrophil recruitment, produces a subepidermal split just above the lamina densa. Because the target lies deep within the basement-membrane zone, autoantibodies localise to the dermal side of salt-split skin, mimicking epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, yet the target and clinical behaviour differ. The frequent coexistence with psoriasis suggests that epidermal inflammation and basement-membrane remodelling may expose or alter the antigen and trigger autoimmunity.
additionalDifferentials: dyshidrosiform bullous eruptions of the palms and soles
additionalInvestigations: perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (linear IgG and C3 at the basement-membrane zone)
lesional biopsy for histopathology (subepidermal blister with neutrophil-rich infiltrate)
indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin (dermal-side binding)
immunoblotting of serum against dermal extract to identify the 200 kDa band
ELISA or immunoblot for laminin gamma-1 reactivity where available
serological exclusion of BP180, BP230 and type VII collagen antibodies
redFlags: extensive blistering with erosions predisposing to secondary infection and fluid loss
diagnostic uncertainty with epidermolysis bullosa acquisita delaying appropriate therapy
complications of systemic immunosuppression in older or comorbid patients
reference.prognosis: The disease usually responds favourably to corticosteroid-based therapy and generally follows a more benign, treatment-responsive course than epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, although relapses may occur on tapering.
pitfalls: Labelling dermal-binding pemphigoid as epidermolysis bullosa acquisita without immunoblot confirmation.
Assuming routine direct immunofluorescence can distinguish anti-p200 disease from other pemphigoids.
Overlooking coexisting psoriasis that may influence management choices.
Failing to send serum for specialised immunoblotting, leaving the diagnosis presumptive.
Attributing acral blistering solely to friction or dyshidrotic eczema.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
management: Topical or systemic corticosteroids to suppress blistering, to which the disease usually responds favourably
Steroid-sparing agents such as dapsone or a tetracycline antibiotic with nicotinamide for maintenance and to limit corticosteroid exposure
Identify and treat associated psoriasis, which may accompany or precede the eruption
Wound and skin care of erosions and blisters to promote healing and prevent secondary infection
Escalate refractory disease to broader immunosuppression under dermatology supervision
Monitor for relapse on corticosteroid tapering with ongoing dermatology follow-up
